FrMS88-de2114-d1e111.summary: Poses the fourth question: whether the subject of the first complex principle has the same formal notion in God and creature according to the real sciences. The negative argument cites Dionysius: negations about God are true, affirmations inadequate.
claims: Dionysius holds negations about God true and affirmations inadequate.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e124.summary: Gives the contrary from Dionysius: creatures are participations of God.
claims: Creatures are participations of God.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e129.summary: Introduces four foundations and develops the first, from the nature of distinction. Things distinguished by their priors (definitional or first-mode per se predicates) differ in formal notion; things distinguished only by posteriors agree in their priors and share a formal notion. Being in God and creature is distinguished precisely by posteriors — dependent/independent, necessary/possible, finite/infinite — since a creature is a being before it is dependent (the absolute precedes the relation), and so God is a being before he is independent; degree is posterior to quiddity, and necessary and contingent are modes of quiddity.
claims: Things distinguished only by posterior features agree in their formal notion.
God and creature are distinguished as beings only by posterior modes such as dependence, necessity, and finitude.
Degree is posterior to quiddity; necessary and contingent are modes of quiddity.
concepts: first mode of per se predication

FrMS88-de2114-d1e199.summary: Adds that things distinguished only by dividing differences share a formal notion in the undivided; God and creature are such.
claims: What is distinguished only by dividing differences shares a common undivided notion.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e207.summary: Second foundation, from the nature of opposition, beginning with relative opposites: things in which a relation of similarity is founded are one in some notion; the creature is similar to God according to the image; similarity, a relation of the first mode, is founded on unity of notion.
claims: Similarity between creature and God (as image) requires a shared notion.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e223.summary: Argument from contrary opposites: contraries are always reduced to a common presupposed element, and contraries belong to God and creature.
claims: Contraries presuppose something common.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e232.summary: Argument from privative opposites: when privations are of the same notion, the corresponding positives are or can be; incorruptibility (privation of corruptibility without aptitude) belongs alike to God, the intellective soul, and the heavens.
claims: Privations of the same notion imply positives of the same notion.
Incorruptibility belongs to God and certain creatures under the same notion.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e254.summary: Argument from contradictory opposites: God and creature (e.g. an angel) are both non-white, and this negation is of the same notion.
claims: Common negations of God and creatures are of the same notion.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e261.summary: Third foundation, from the nature of plurality: things said to be many according to one numbered thing share a common notion; man and ox are counted not as 'two men' or 'two oxen' but as 'two animals'; God and creature are called two beings.
claims: God and creatures are counted as two beings, implying a common notion of being.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e285.summary: Second argument from plurality: no equivocal is numbered in its equivocates, but only by several significations of the word; being is pluralized in God and creature, as they are several beings.
claims: Equivocals are not numbered in their equivocates; being is.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e297.summary: Third argument: things which, with everything outside their quiddity removed, are entirely the same have the same formal notion; plurality is not of the quidditative notion of God, creature, or being, so with plurality removed they would be the same being.
claims: Plurality is not part of the quiddity of God, creature, or being.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e310.summary: Fourth argument: things to which all plurality is adventitious are of the same formal notion, and God and creature are such, according to Augustine, De Trinitate VIII.
claims: Plurality is adventitious to God and creature.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e317.summary: Fourth foundation, from the nature of perfection: every pure perfection (perfectio simpliciter) found in a creature is in God under the same formal notion, since the most perfect being must have every pure perfection (he is that than which nothing greater can be thought). Being is a pure perfection because it is included in many pure perfections, is neither limited nor unlimited of itself, is better than anything incompossible with it (only nothing), and is prior to its attributes, some of which are pure perfections.
claims: Every pure perfection in creatures is in God under the same formal notion.
Being is a pure perfection.

FrMS88-de2114-d1e359.summary: Reply to Dionysius: he speaks of transferred or metaphorical affirmations.
claims: Dionysius' denial of affirmations concerns metaphorical predicates.

FrMS88-de2114.summary: The fourth question of the prologue asks whether the subject of the first complex principle (being) has the same formal notion in God and creature according to the real sciences, complementing the sermocinal approach of question 3. Against Dionysius' claim that negations of God are true and affirmations inadequate, Meyronnes builds four 'foundations'. From the nature of distinction: things distinguished only by what is posterior to their formal notion agree in that notion, and God and creature, as being, are distinguished only by posterior modes such as dependent/independent, necessary/possible, and finite/infinite (degree being posterior to quiddity), or by dividing differences. From the nature of opposition: relative opposites (similarity, as the creature is God's image), contraries, privative opposites (incorruptibility in God, the soul, and the heavens), and contradictories (non-white) all presuppose a common notion. From the nature of plurality: God and creature are counted as 'two beings', which no equivocal permits; removing plurality, which is not of their quiddity, leaves the same being. From the nature of perfection: every pure perfection found in creatures is in God under the same formal notion, and being is a pure perfection (neither limited nor unlimited, better than whatever is incompossible with it, prior to perfect attributes). He answers that Dionysius speaks of transferred or metaphorical affirmations.
claims: Things distinguished only by what is posterior to their formal notion share that notion; God and creature are so distinguished as beings.
Finite and infinite, necessary and contingent, are intrinsic modes or degrees posterior to the quiddity of being.
Relations of similarity, contrariety, privation, and contradiction between God and creatures presuppose a common notion.
God and creatures are numbered as 'two beings', which presupposes a univocal notion.
Being is a pure perfection and so is found in God under the same formal notion as in creatures.
Dionysius' denial of affirmations concerns metaphorical predications.
